segments.translit: tam eva mahāsukharājānaṃ svānandāsavapānapramodamanasā kukkurīpādāḥ sandhyābhāṣayā prakaṭayitum āhuḥ |
segments.translation: His mind delighted by drinking the liquor of his own bliss, [Kukkurīpāda]{p-kukkuri} speaks in order to make that same king of [great bliss]{mahasukha} manifest in [twilight language]{sandhya-bhasa}.
segments.note: Munidatta introduces the song: his mind delighted by drinking the liquor of his own bliss, [Kukkurīpāda]{p-kukkuri} sets out to make that same king of [great bliss]{mahasukha} plain in [twilight language]{sandhya-bhasa}.

flags.note: mahāsukharājānam can be 'the king, great bliss' (great bliss as the king) or 'the king of great bliss'. I chose the second, which is how the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) reads it: bde ba chen po'i rgyal po. 'That same' (tam eva) looks back to the great bliss of the comment on song 1.

The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has rang gi chang gi btung bas, 'by drinking his own liquor', with nothing for ānanda, 'bliss'. It renders sandhyābhāṣā as dgongs pa'i skad, 'intentional language', its usual rendering, which takes the word as sandhā-.

segments.translit:
dulītyādi — dvayākāraṃ yasmin līnaṃ gataṃ mahāsukhakamalaṃ | dulisandhyāsaṅkete boddha(dha)vyaṃ | karmmamudrāprasaṅgāt ānandādikramadvāreṇa tasya dohanaṃ saṃvṛttibodhicittaṃ tat avadhūtīmā[5]rgeṇa gatvā pīṭhake vajramaṇau patat dharaṇaṃ na yāti | bālayoginas tasya dharaṇe na samarthāḥ ||
tathā ca kṛṣṇācāryyapādāḥ —
ehu se dudharaṇa dharaṇidhara samaviṣama uttāraṇa pāvai |
bhaṇai kāhnu dullabbhyā duravagāha ko maṇe paribhāvai ||
tasmāt gurupāramparyyakramajanitayogīndrāḥ kāyavṛkṣasya phalaṃ tad eva bodhicittaṃ ciñcāphalavat vakraṃ | kumbhīram iti | vilakṣaṇapariśodhitakumbhakasamādhinā svānubhavakrameṇa ca tasya bhakṣaṇaṃ niḥsvabhāvīkaraṇaṃ kurvvanti |
segments.translation:
‘The [tortoise]{tortoise} milked…’ and so on: the [lotus]{lotus} of [great bliss]{mahasukha}, in which the dual aspect has dissolved. ‘Duli’ is to be understood as a code word of [twilight language]{sandhya-bhasa}. What is milked from it through union with a [karmamudrā]{karmamudra}, by way of the sequence of joys beginning with [joy]{ananda}, is [conventional]{samvrti} [bodhicitta]{bodhicitta}. That travels by the path of the [avadhūtī]{avadhuti} and, falling into the [stool]{pitha}, the [vajra jewel]{vajramani}, cannot be held. Novice [yogis]{yogi} are not able to hold it.
And so the master [Kāṇha]{p-kanha} says:
This is that mountain, hard to hold;
through it one gains the crossing over even and uneven.
Kāṇha says: hard to win, hard to fathom,
who can ponder it in the mind?
Hence the [lords of yogis]{yogindra}, brought forth in succession through the [guru's lineage]{guru-sampradaya}: the fruit of the body-[tree]{tree} is that same bodhicitta, crooked like a [tamarind]{tamarind} pod. ‘The [crocodile]{crocodile}’: through the [samādhi]{samadhi} of [kumbhaka]{kumbhaka} purified by [vilakṣaṇa]{vilaksana}, and through the stages of their own experience, they eat it, that is, they make it [without intrinsic nature]{nihsvabhava}.
segments.note: Munidatta reads the [tortoise]{tortoise} as the lotus of great bliss, where duality dissolves; its milk is conventional bodhicitta, drawn through the joys in union with a karmamudrā; once it falls into the [stool]{pitha}, the vajra jewel, novices cannot hold it. The [tamarind]{tamarind} is bodhicitta, fruit of the body-tree; the [crocodile]{crocodile}, kumbhaka samādhi, eats it, making it without intrinsic nature.

equations.en: the lotus of great bliss, in which the dual aspect has dissolved
conventional bodhicitta, drawn out through the sequence of joys in union with a karmamudrā
the vajra jewel
the body, as the body-tree
bodhicitta, the fruit of the body-tree, crooked like a tamarind pod
the samādhi of kumbhaka purified by vilakṣaṇa
making it without intrinsic nature

citations.quoted: This is that mountain, hard to hold; through it one gains the crossing over even and uneven. Kāṇha says: hard to win, hard to fathom, who can ponder it in the mind?
citations.work: A verse of Kāṇha (Kṛṣṇācārya), as Munidatta names him; the work is not named

flags.note: The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) spells out the syllable play that the Sanskrit only implies: du ni gnyid kyi rnam pa / li ni gang la thim par 'gyur te, 'du is the aspect of gnyid' (gnyid, 'sleep', is probably a slip for gnyis, 'two'), 'li is that into which it dissolves'. It then adds du li ni rus sbal te, 'duli is the tortoise', which the Sanskrit never says. For the lotus it has bde ba chen po'i rnam pa pad+ma, 'the lotus, the form of great bliss'.

The Tibetan has kun rdzob byang chub kyi sems de a wa d+hU tI'i lam gyis 'ong ba'o, 'that conventional bodhicitta comes by the path of the avadhūtī' (the Sanskrit gatvā is 'having gone'). It also has stegs bu ni rdo rje nor bu las ltung na gzung du med pa, 'the stool: if it falls from the vajra jewel, it cannot be held', where the Sanskrit locative says 'falling into the stool, the vajra jewel'. Either way, bodhicitta that has fallen cannot be kept.

Kāṇha's Apabhraṃśa verse is obscure and probably corrupt. I take dullabbhyā as dullabha, 'hard to win' (Sanskrit durlabha). The Tibetan mtshon dka', 'hard to point out', suggests durlakṣya. For duravagāha, 'hard to fathom', the Tibetan has brjod dka', 'hard to express'. In line 1 I take samaviṣama uttāraṇa pāvai as 'gains the crossing over even and uneven'. The Tibetan has mnyam dang mi mnyam 'dzin par byed, 'holds the even and the uneven', as if it read a word for 'holding' in place of uttāraṇa. dharaṇidhara, 'earth-bearer', is taken as 'mountain', as the Tibetan ri bo also has it; it also plays on dudharaṇa, 'hard to hold'.

In the sentence beginning tasmāt, yogīndrāḥ gets no verb until kurvanti at the end of the next sentence: the gloss on the tamarind and the lemma kumbhīram iti come in between. I kept the break with a colon rather than smoothing it over. The Tibetan supplies a verb, rnal 'byor gyi dbang phyug rnams kyis shes te, 'the lords of yogis know', perhaps reading -jñāta- where the Sanskrit has -janita-.
The Tibetan, bse yab kyi 'bras bu bzhin du yod pa'o, 'is like the fruit of the bse yab', has nothing for vakra, 'crooked'. The likeness in crookedness rests on the Sanskrit alone.
gurupāramparyakrama is 'the succession of the guru lineage'. The word is pāramparya, not sampradāya, but I linked it to guru-sampradaya as the same idea. The Tibetan has bla ma brgyud pa'i rim pa.

segments.translit:
dhruvapadena dṛḍhīkurvvann āha —
aṅganam iti | vyutthānavātam utprekṣāpraveśañ ca boddhavyaṃ | viātīti ātmani pariśuddhāvadhūtīrūpam adhimucya yogīndro vadati bhoḥ pariśuddhāvadhūtīke śṛṇu prathamaṃ vajrajāpopadeśena viramānandāvadhūtīgṛham ubhayaṃ naya | tasmin gṛhe punar arddharātrau caturthīsandhyāyāṃ kāneṭa ityādi | tad eva praveśādivātadoṣavibhavaṃ sahajānandacaureṇa hṛtaṃ |
segments.translation:
Making this firm with the [refrain]{dhruvapada}, he says:
‘The [courtyard]{courtyard}’: this is to be understood as the [wind]{vayu} of [emergence]{vyutthana} and, figuratively, as entering. ‘[Biātī]{biati}’: having resolved upon the form of the purified [avadhūtī]{avadhuti} in himself, the [lord of yogis]{yogindra} says, ‘O purified avadhūtī, listen! First, by the [instruction]{upadesa} in [vajra recitation]{vajrajapa}, lead both into the [house]{house} of the avadhūtī of the [joy of cessation]{viramananda}.’ Then, in that house, at [midnight]{ardharatri}, the fourth juncture: ‘The [earring]{kaneta}…’ and so on. That is just the wealth of the faults of the winds, beginning with entering, stolen by the [thief]{thief}, [innate joy]{sahajananda}.
segments.note: Munidatta hears the [lord of yogis]{yogindra} addressing the purified avadhūtī. The [courtyard]{courtyard} is the wind of emergence, with entering; by vajra recitation both are led into the house of the avadhūtī of the joy of cessation (Tibetan: ‘joy of variety’). At midnight, the fourth juncture, the [thief]{thief}, innate joy, steals the [earring]{kaneta}: the wealth of the winds' faults.

equations.en: the wind of emergence, and entering
the purified avadhūtī, whom the lord of yogis addresses
the fourth juncture (caturthī sandhyā)
the wealth of the faults of the winds, beginning with entering
innate joy

flags.note: vyutthānavātam utprekṣāpraveśañ ca: the compound utprekṣā-praveśa is odd. I take utprekṣā as the poetic figure (Munidatta uses the word that way in song 1): 'the wind of emergence and, figuratively, entering'. It could instead be a gerund, utprekṣya, 'considering it', or a corruption of apekṣya, 'with reference to it'. The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) supports the last: 'byung ba'i rlung la nye bar ltos nas 'jug pa yang, 'with reference to the wind of arising, entering too'.

For ātmani ... adhimucya, 'having resolved upon (the form of the purified avadhūtī) in himself', the Tibetan has bdag nyid yongs su dag pa'i a wa d+hU tI'i tshul du grol ba, 'himself liberated in the manner of the purified avadhūtī'. grol ba suggests the translators read or understood vimucya.

The Tibetan has sna tshogs pa'i dga' ba a wa d+hU tI'i khang par gnyis po len pa'o, 'the two are taken into the house of the avadhūtī, the joy of variety'. 'Joy of variety' (sna tshogs is the usual word for vicitra) stands where the Sanskrit has viramānanda, 'joy of cessation'. The Tibetan also puts this as a statement, not the imperative naya, 'lead'.

prathamaṃ ... naya may continue the lord of yogis' words to the avadhūtī, or it may be Munidatta's instruction to the reader. I kept it inside the address because the imperative follows śṛṇu directly and seems to gloss the refrain's 'courtyard ... house'. ubhayam, 'both', presumably means the winds of emergence and entering, but he does not say so.

The Tibetan de la khang pa ni slar yang nam phyed la bzhi pa'i mtshams so, 'there, the house is again midnight, the fourth juncture', makes the house itself the time, where the Sanskrit has 'in that house, at midnight'. Other small differences: the lemma for the courtyard is sgo mdun, 'in front of the door', but the Tibetan's quotation of the song has sgo bdun, 'seven doors'; the lemma for biātī is rigs ngan, 'low-born woman'; bstan par, 'to teach', stands for dṛḍhīkurvan, 'making firm' (perhaps a slip for brtan par); and dngos po rnams, 'things', stands for vibhava.

vibhava can mean 'wealth, property' or 'unfolding, manifestation'; I chose 'wealth' because it is what the thief steals. caturthī sandhyā is the fourth of the day's junctures (dawn, noon, dusk, midnight). It is the same word sandhyā as in 'twilight language', but a different sense. Munidatta writes viātī; I use the glossary form biātī.

segments.translit:
dvitī[5ka]yapadena tam evārthaṃ pratinirddeśayati |
sasuretyādi tvaritādiśvāsaṃ caturthāna[ndaṃ] yoganidrāṃ nītvā 'vadhūtīśabdasandhyayā anādibhavavikalpañ ca dhutvā prakṛtipariśuddhāvadhūtīrūpeṇa yoginyo 'py aharnniśaṃ jāgaraṇaṃ kurvvanti | kāneṭṭa prabhāsvaracoreṇa praveśādivātadoṣo yadā nītas tadā grāhyādyabhāve yogīndro daśadiśi kvāpi kiñcin na prārthayati |
segments.translation:
With the second [verse]{pada} he points out the same meaning again.
‘The [father-in-law]{father-in-law}…’ and so on: having led the breath, beginning with the ‘swift’, into [yogic sleep]{yoganidra}, the fourth [joy]{ananda}, and having shaken off, as the word [avadhūtī]{avadhuti} says in [twilight language]{sandhya-bhasa}, the [conceptual thought]{vikalpa} of beginningless existence, the [yoginīs]{yogini} too, in the form of the naturally purified avadhūtī, keep awake day and night. ‘The [earring]{kaneta}’: when the fault of the [winds]{vayu}, beginning with entering, has been carried off by the [thief]{thief}, [clear light]{prabhasvara}, then, since the grasped and the rest are absent, the [lord of yogis]{yogindra} asks for nothing anywhere in the ten directions.
segments.note: Munidatta reads the sleeping [father-in-law]{father-in-law} as the breath, beginning with the ‘swift’, led into yogic sleep, the fourth joy (Tibetan: ‘joy of peace’); the wakeful [bride]{bride} as yoginīs who, as the naturally purified avadhūtī, have ‘shaken off’ concepts. The [thief]{thief} is clear light: once it takes the winds' fault, nothing grasped remains, and the lord of yogis wants nothing.

equations.en: the breath, beginning with the ‘swift’, led into yogic sleep, the fourth joy
having shaken off (dhutvā) the conceptual thought of beginningless existence
the yoginīs, in the form of the naturally purified avadhūtī, keeping awake day and night
the fault of the winds, beginning with entering
clear light

flags.note: caturthāna[ndaṃ]: the last syllables are Shastri's restoration. The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has zhi ba'i dga' ba'i rnal 'byor gyi gnyid, 'the yogic sleep of the joy of peace', with no 'fourth'.

'vadhūtīśabdasandhyayā: I take it with dhutvā, 'having shaken off', as a pun on avadhūtī, 'she who has shaken off': the yoginīs shake off concepts, as the word avadhūtī says in twilight language. It could instead close the first clause ('led into yogic sleep: so twilight language speaks of the avadhūtī'). The Tibetan reads it that way, a wa d+hU tIr dgongs pa'i skad kyis so, and renders dhutvā as spangs, 'abandoned', so the pun disappears.
tvaritādiśvāsa, 'the breath beginning with the swift', may name the first of a series of breaths. The Tibetan has dang por myur ba'i dbugs, 'first, the swift breath'.

The Tibetan has sgyug mo, 'mother-in-law', for the father-in-law, as in its version of the song. It has rgyas par bshad, 'explains at length', for pratinirdeśayati, 'points out again', and btsal du med, 'there is nothing to seek', for na prārthayati, 'asks for nothing'.

segments.translit:
dvitīyapariśuddhāvadhūtībhedena satyadvayasyānuśaṃsām āha —
divasai ityādi | mṛdvādyadhyāsaya bhedena sā avadhūtīkā saṃvṛttyā śukrarūpeṇa trailokyaṃ nirmmāya punaḥ svayam eva divādijñānam utpādya kāṛai iti | kāyakālapuruṣāya bibheti santrastā bhavati |
tathā cā[ga]maḥ —
yathā citrakaro rūpaṃ yakṣasyātibhayaṅkaraṃ |
samālikhya svayaṃ bhītaḥ saṃsāre hy abudhas tathā ||
rātrīti | prajñājñānena prakṛtipariśuddhāvadhūtikā pañcaskandhādīn abhiṣicya | kāmarur iti | svayam eva mahāsukhacakrasvasthāne nirvvikalpaṃ gacchati | [6]
tathāgamaḥ | svasthānasthaḥ sahajapavanaḥ kalpanājālamuktaḥ
śāntaṃ toṣaṃ kim api janayaty eṣa śūnyasvabhāvaḥ |
asmād gurvvāhitabahukṛpopāyahetor abādhya-
saṃsāre 'smin prabhavati sadānandasattvārthakṛtyaḥ ||
segments.translation:
By distinguishing a second, purified [avadhūtī]{avadhuti}, he speaks in praise of the [two truths]{satyadvaya}.
‘By day…’ and so on: according to the differences of disposition, beginning with the weak, that avadhūtī, [conventionally]{samvrti}, in the form of semen, creates the [three worlds]{trailokya}; then of itself it produces the knowledge of day and so on. ‘A [crow]{crow}’: it is afraid of the [Kālapuruṣa]{kalapurusa} of the body and becomes terrified. And so scripture says:
As a painter who has drawn a [yakṣa]{yaksa}'s form, utterly terrifying,
is himself afraid, so is the fool in [saṃsāra]{samsara}.
‘Night’: the naturally purified avadhūtī, through [wisdom-knowledge]{prajnajnana}, [empowers]{abhiseka} the five [aggregates]{skandha} and the rest. ‘[Kāmaru]{pl-kamaru}’: of itself, free of [concepts]{vikalpa}, it goes to its own place in the [wheel of great bliss]{mahasukha-cakra}.
And so scripture says:
Abiding in its own place, freed from the net of concepts, the [innate]{sahaja} [wind]{vayu},
whose nature is [emptiness]{sunyata}, brings forth a peaceful contentment beyond words.
From this, by reason of the means of great [compassion]{karuna} instilled by the [guru]{guru},
he comes forth in this saṃsāra, which is not to be set aside, his work the welfare of beings in constant joy.
segments.note: Munidatta reads the couplet as praising the two truths through the avadhūtī's two forms. By day, conventionally, as semen, it creates the three worlds and fears the [crow]{crow}, the bodily [Kālapuruṣa]{kalapurusa}, like a painter afraid of his own yakṣa. At night, purified, it empowers the aggregates and goes to [Kāmaru]{pl-kamaru}, its own place in the wheel of great bliss.

equations.en: the avadhūtī: by day, conventionally, in the form of semen; at night, naturally purified
the Kālapuruṣa of the body, whom she fears
the avadhūtī's own place in the wheel of great bliss

citations.quoted: As a painter who has drawn a yakṣa's form, utterly terrifying, is himself afraid, so is the fool in saṃsāra.
citations.work: Scripture (āgama), not named by Munidatta; possibly the Cittaviśuddhiprakaraṇa ascribed to Āryadeva

citations.quoted: Abiding in its own place, freed from the net of concepts, the innate wind, whose nature is emptiness, brings forth a peaceful contentment beyond words. From this, by reason of the means of great compassion instilled by the guru, he comes forth in this saṃsāra, which is not to be set aside, his work the welfare of beings in constant joy.
citations.work: Scripture (āgama), not named by Munidatta; not identified

flags.note: dvitīya-: by Munidatta's own count couplet 4 is his third verse (he has just called couplet 3 his second), and the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has rkang pa gsum pas yongs su dag pa a wa d+hU tI'i dbye bas, 'with the third verse, by the division of the purified avadhūtī'. The Sanskrit probably once read tṛtīyapadena pariśuddhāvadhūtībhedena. I have translated the printed text ('by distinguishing a second, purified avadhūtī'), which gives a sense but may be a corruption.
adhyāsaya stands for adhyāśaya, 'disposition', which the Tibetan lhag pa'i bsam pa confirms. Munidatta does not say what the dispositions 'beginning with the weak' (weak, middling, strong) belong to.
kāyakālapuruṣa can be 'the Kālapuruṣa of the body' or 'the body, the Kālapuruṣa'. The Tibetan dus kyi skyes bu, 'the person of time', has no 'body'.

For saṃvṛtyā śukrarūpeṇa, 'conventionally, in the form of semen', the Tibetan has kun rdzob byang chub kyi sems kyi gzugs kyis, 'in the form of conventional bodhicitta'. For divādijñāna it has nyin mo'i rnam par shes pa, 'the consciousness of day'. Its shes rab ye shes kyi rang bzhin rnam par dag pa'i a wa d+hU tI pa'i phung po lnga, 'the five aggregates of the purified avadhūtī whose nature is wisdom-knowledge', makes wisdom-knowledge the avadhūtī's nature rather than the means of empowering.

The Tibetan gives only the first half of the second quoted verse as verse (rang gnas gnas la lhan skyes kyi ...). The second half comes as prose: de'i phyir bla mas gnang ba'i snying rje chen po'i thabs kyi rgyu mnos pas 'khor ba 'dir rab tu skyes shing rtag tu dga' bas sems can gyi don mdzad do, 'therefore, having received the cause, the means of great compassion granted by the guru, he is born in this saṃsāra and with constant joy acts for beings'. It has the honorific mdzad and no closing zhes, so it may take these lines as Munidatta's own. It has nothing for abādhya.

abādhya-saṃsāre: I took this as 'in this saṃsāra, which is not to be set aside' (bādh-, 'reject, annul'). It could also mean 'which cannot harm him'. anuśaṃsā is 'praise', as the Tibetan rjes su bsngags pa has it; in Buddhist Sanskrit it can also mean 'benefit'.

segments.translit:
atidaurlabhyapratipādanā[ya] caturthapadam āha —
aisanītyādi | īdṛśy atīvaniṣprapañcacaryyā yogīndrasya sthitir vviharaṇādikaṃ kukkurīpādenaivābhihitaṃ | asyārtho yogikoṭīnāṃ madhye yady ekayogihṛdaye 'ntarbhavatīti |
tathā ca kṛṣṇācāryyapādāḥ —
loa gavva samuvvahai haum̐ paramathe pavīṇa
koṛia majhem̐ eku jai hoi nirañjanalīna ||2||
segments.translation:
To show how extremely rare this is, he speaks the fourth [verse]{pada}.
‘Such…’ and so on: such [conduct]{carya}, utterly free of [elaboration]{prapanca}, the abiding, moving about and so on of the [lord of yogis]{yogindra}, has been told by [Kukkurīpāda]{p-kukkuri} himself. Its meaning is: among ten million [yogis]{yogi}, it enters the heart of a single yogi, if it does at all.
And so the master [Kāṇha]{p-kanha} says:
People carry their pride: ‘I am skilled in the [ultimate]{paramartha}.’
Among ten million, one, if any, becomes absorbed in [the stainless]{niranjana}.
segments.note: Munidatta says the last couplet shows how rare this is: the lord of yogis' [conduct]{carya}, utterly free of elaboration, which [Kukkurīpāda]{p-kukkuri} sings, enters the heart of one yogi in ten million, if any. Kāṇha's verse makes the same point: many pride themselves on knowing the ultimate, but hardly one in ten million is absorbed in the stainless.

equations.en: the lord of yogis' abiding, moving about and so on, utterly free of elaboration
ten million yogis

citations.quoted: People carry their pride: ‘I am skilled in the ultimate.’ Among ten million, one, if any, becomes absorbed in the stainless.
citations.work: A verse of Kāṇha (Kṛṣṇācārya), as Munidatta names him; perhaps from his Dohākoṣa (not verified)

flags.note: yady ... antarbhavati, 'if it enters': I take the conditional as stressing rarity ('if it does at all'), as Kāṇha's jai, 'if', does in the verse he quotes. The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) makes it a question: gcig gi snying gi nang du 'jug srid dam, 'could it enter the heart of even one?'. Its version of line 5b is also a question (gcig snying 'jug srid dam). Both read the line as doubt or rarity, where the current draft of 5b is a plain statement.

The Tibetan has spros pa med pa spyod pa'i glu, 'the song of conduct free of elaboration', adding 'song' (glu) as in its version of 5a. It renders sthiti as brtan par byed, 'makes firm', and viharaṇa as spyod pa. In Kāṇha's verse it has nga yis don dam shes so snyam, 'thinking: I know the ultimate', and mig sman med pa'i mi snang 'gyur, 'becomes invisible, without eye-salve', a literal rendering of nirañjana-līna.
Munidatta writes aisanī for the song's aisana. The ||2|| after Kāṇha's verse marks the end of the comment on song 2 and is not translated.

questions: cp.02.m5 opens with dvitīya-, but Munidatta's own count and the Tibetan (rkang pa gsum pas, 'with the third verse') both point to tṛtīyapadena. I translated the printed text ('by distinguishing a second, purified avadhūtī'). Should we emend to 'With the third verse, by distinguishing the purified avadhūtī, …'?

cp.02.5b: Munidatta paraphrases the line with yadi ('it enters the heart of one yogi in ten million, if it does at all') and quotes Kāṇha's jai ('if') to make the point of rarity. The Tibetan line reads bye ba'i nang na gcig snying 'jug srid dam, 'among ten million, could it enter one heart?'. The current draft, 'Among ten million, it has entered one heart', is a plain statement. Should the line or its note be revisited?

cp.02.m3: I kept prathamaṃ … naya ('first … lead both into the house') inside the lord of yogis' words to the avadhūtī. Is it better read as Munidatta's own instruction? The Tibetan also names the house's joy sna tshogs pa'i dga' ba, 'joy of variety', in place of viramānanda; I put that in the note. Keep it there, or leave it to the flags?
cp.02.m3 utprekṣāpraveśañ ca: I rendered it 'figuratively, as entering'. Would you prefer the Tibetan-supported 'with reference to it, entering too' (apekṣya)?
cp.02.m2, Kāṇha's verse: keep 'hard to win' (dullabha), or follow the Tibetan's mtshon dka', 'hard to point out' (durlakṣya)?

Term choices: I used [Kāṇha]{p-kanha} for Munidatta's Kṛṣṇācāryapāda ('the master Kāṇha'), [biātī]{biati} for his spelling viātī, [conventionally]{samvrti} and [empowers]{abhiseka} as inflected surfaces, and linked gurupāramparya to guru-sampradaya. Are these acceptable?

cp.02.m4: 'the fourth joy' depends on Shastri's restoration caturthā[nandaṃ]; the Tibetan has zhi ba'i dga' ba, 'joy of peace'. Should the glossary entries for yogic sleep and father-in-law, which say 'the fourth joy', mention that it is a restoration?
